title: Catching a want at its source
hookLine: Bhairava says to see a desire as it rises, and trace it back home
carry: iccha shakti: even wanting has a sacred source
tomorrow: what do strangers on a crowded train already share?
last: A SNEEZE CAN BE A DOOR.

lines: A FIRST FLICKER: I WANT THAT.
cards: A phone buzzes, and the hand is already reaching. A bakery smell drifts past, and the feet have half turned. Before the reach and the turn there was a first flicker: I want that.
It's fast, and it usually goes straight into action. So what if you caught a want before it turned into a plan? The Vijnana Bhairava says to slow down right there, at the flicker.

teach.h: SEE THE WANT AS IT ARISES.
teach.b: When a desire arises, Bhairava says, see it arising, and end it right then, at its start. Then the mind settles back into the very place the desire came from. The Sanskrit word is iccha, wanting.
Notice what isn't said. Nothing here calls wanting wicked, or the person weak. On this path, wanting has a surprising pedigree.

teach.h: ICCHA: WILL, A POWER OF SHIVA.
teach.b: Kashmir Shaiva teachers name three powers of Shiva: iccha, will; jnana, knowing; and kriya, doing. Iccha shakti, the power to will, is the first of them.
A two a.m. wish for something is a small, scattered spark of that power. So the practice doesn't fight it.
Caught early, before it's a plan, a purchase or a grudge, it's traced back home, and for a moment the attention lands where it began, quiet and open.
A neighboring verse turns it into a question: before a desire or a thought has arisen, what am I?
Now hold the week up. A householder's day, every act offered. A body made ready with sacred sound.
God with form and beyond it. The goddess rising and falling as breath. Om, fading into silence.
A sneeze, met with praise in one tradition and stillness in this one. And the first flicker of a want.

teach.h: CATCH THE MOMENT AT ITS EDGE.
teach.b: Different doors, one move: catch the moment at its edge, and rest in what was there before it.

how: Some meditators who study the Vijnana Bhairava practice watching a desire at its first appearance and letting it go, in sitting practice and in the course of the day.

o: fighting each desire until it finally gives up
giving in to wants so they lose their pull
seeing a want arise, and letting it settle back

games.q: the want, caught early. tap the pairs.
p: will, knowing, doing: Shiva's three powers

s: the Vijnana Bhairava calls desire shameful
nothing in the verse shames the wanting; Kashmir Shaiva teachers even count will, iccha, among Shiva's powers.
a verse asks: before a desire or a thought arises, what am I?
the neighbor of the desire practice.

games.q: your little brother sees candy at the checkout and his hand is already out. what would this dharana notice first?
o: the first flicker of wanting, before the hand moved.
the candy, since the trouble is what's in front of him.
the guilt afterward, since that's what teaches him.
games.why: the practice catches the want as it arises, before it becomes a reach, and lets the mind settle where it came from. no shame in it.

practice: Sit still, eyes closed if that's comfortable, and wait for the first small want to show up: to shift, to scratch, to check a phone. When it comes, see it arriving, and let it go before it moves you. Rest in the quiet it came from.

wordCard.voice: The Vijnana Bhairava: here, iccha, a want seen as it arises, let go at once, and the quiet it came from.

carryVoice: Carry this: iccha shakti, even wanting has a sacred source. A week of doors, gathered.

sources.ref: Vijnana Bhairava, the dharana on a desire seen as it arises, ended at once, and dissolved in its source
